##### SECTION 1:  INTRODUCTION 

In this report we provide an Executive Summary which gives an overview of the he outlook for the copper industry.  A brief outline of our approach in forecasting output and the main definitions are provided below. 

###### Note on Methodology 

In the supply analysis, forecasts of mine and smelter production to 2020 are composed of three elements; firstly, “ base case ” production capability or capacity; secondly, highly probable projects ; and thirdly, a further production adjustment . 

- Base case production capability or capacity comprises existing operations, along with expansions or greenfield projects that are under construction or that have received board approval and that have been financed. 

- Highly probable projects do not meet these strict criteria for inclusion as base case capacity but, in Brook Hunt’s judgement, will most likely proceed within the time frame indicated. 

- In order to maintain an orderly market a production adjustment is made taking into ac

count price levels, industry cost structure, concentrate availability, TC/RCs etc.  Where the production adjustment is positive, i.e. there is a need for further mine/smelter/refinery production over and above base case and highly probable output, implicit reference is made to the existence of other projects, both probable and possible, in order to assess whether there are enough projects sufficiently far advanced in their exploration/development to fill the potential supply gap.  If base case plus highly probable supply is expected to exceed forecast demand, then a _negative_ adjustment to output may be made in order to prevent the build up of unrealistically large inventories.  Typically, lower prices will be the catalyst for this action and will be reflected in the market forecast.  Reference is made to the industry cost structure to determine the likely level of production loss at specific price levels.

##### SECTION 2:  EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 

- Reflecting a gloomier outlook for copper we have made a number of revisions to our global consumption figures.  The net effect of these changes is that we have lowered our global demand estimates markedly throughout the forecast period.  In the near term we have lowered our consumption figures by a net 0.8Mt for 2009, 2010 and 2011 respectively.  We now forecast that global copper consumption will decrease by 4.5% from 18.0Mt in 2008 to 17.2Mt in 2009.  In 2010 we project that global demand will rise by 1.4% to 17.3Mt and we expect annual growth to rise to 6.3% in 2011 bringing global refined consumption to 18.4Mt.  Over the forecast period we expect that global refined copper consumption will increase by 2.3% p.a. from 2009 to 2020, a rise in absolute terms of 6.3Mt.  Most of the mature copper consuming regions are expected to show either minimal or negative growth in demand over the period, with the increase driven mainly by China and other developing Asian countries. 

- Global copper mine production capability totalled ~15.6Mt in 2008 with 12.6Mt derived from concentrates and 3Mt from SxEw.  In 2009, global mine production capability (before disruption allowance) is forecast to grow by 3.5% to just over 16.1Mt.  During the forecast period 2009–2020 we project that global base case copper mine production capability (excluding highly probable and probable projects) will fall by 1.3% p.a. 

- Based on current production plans, the transition from growth to contraction in our base case mine output is expected by 2013 as production is lost either to mine closures or grade attrition exceeding committed incremental expansion or committed new project capacity.  Base case mine production capability is thus forecast to decline by 3% p.a. between 2013 (inclusive) and 2020, falling from a peak of ~17.7Mt in 2012 to just over 13.9Mt in 2020.  At the same time, demand for additional mine production to meet increased market requirements for refi

ned metal will create an implied shortfall in base case mine output of ~0.9Mt in 2014, ~2.7Mt/a in 2017 and ~5.7Mt/a by 2020. 

- We estimate that global copper smelter production was 14.3Mt/a in 2008 (+1.8%) and forecast that production capability will reach 14.8Mt in 2009 (+3.7%) and 16.4Mt in 2010 (+10.7%). 

- Our estimated global market surplus for 2008 stands at ~410kt, little changed from our previous estimate with stocks, at 48 days of consumption, remaining below normal levels of 60-65 days.  We believe that sizeable metal surpluses will remain a feature of the market in 2009 and 2010 in the light of anticipated weak demand in most regions.  We forecast that copper prices will continue to weaken with the cyclical low being reached in 2010.  As a result we anticipate that in nominal terms copper prices will average $3636/t (or $1.65/lb) this year and slightly below $3090/t ($1.40/lb) in 2010.  By the time we enter 2011, prices should reflect the new reality of recovering demand in a tight market, and will respond accordingly, rising to $3490/t ($1.58/lb) in that year. 

- We forecast that global industrial production growth will average 2.8% over the period 2009-2020.  Mature economy IP is expected to grow by an average of just 1.2% over the period while developing IP is forecast to increase by a much stronger 6.1% p.a.

##### SECTION 3:  DEMAND ANALYSIS 

The economic crisis that is now clearly affecting metals demand globally could, in retrospect, have been detected in select consuming nations, such as the USA, as early as late-2007, and copper demand in the Western World at least contracted then by 1.6% to 12.1Mt.  On the whole, however, the more positive news of ongoing Chinese expansion carried the day, and globally copper demand increased by 2.7% that year, making it the second straight year of such growth rates.  Bearish tendencies held sway as we entered 2008 though, and by Q3 virtually all nations were beginning to detect the signs of a concerted slow down even if a complete awareness of the impending financial crisis had yet to dawn.  The collapse in the final quarter consumed everyone’s attention, and almost all data everywhere would point to a severe downturn in business levels, the likes of which we have not seen since the collection of comparable statistics began in the 1950s.  Western World copper demand fell again, therefore, but this time at almost double the rate of the prior year, at 3.0%, to 11.7Mt.  Even Chinese demand growth in 2008 of 9% year-on-year meant that, globally, copper demand stood still at 17.96Mt. 

_Consumption held at 2007 levels last year with the recessionary characteristics being felt everywhere during H2_ 

This year, with Chinese demand growth at just 5%, and Western World demand contracting by an expected 8-9% year-on-year, we are expecting global copper demand to fall away by 4.5% to just 17.1Mt.  Demand levels into 2010 will

remain subdued, with just 1% growth expected globally (+5% in China, and with the Western World still fighting its way out of crisis at -0.6% contraction), and it is not until 2011 that we can see any real demand growth at all. These two poor years of 2009-2010, however, will probably mean that stocks will have been drawn down, scrap generation rates will be low, and new metal from projects stalled, and so the recovery, once detected, will come swiftly. In 2011, we anticipate global copper demand growth of over 6%, to 18.4Mt, with reasonable growth also expected during the two or three recovery years thereafter. The country’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) reported that copper semis exports during Q4 2008 amounted to just 98kt, vs. 135kt for Q3 and 129kt for Q4 2007. Equally, imports for Q4 2008 came to 187kt vs. 241kt for Q3 and 270kt for Q4 2007, implying quite a dramatic slowdown in Chinese industrial activity. With these trends continuing in place into early 2009, according to January data alone, there has been some concern about the pace of the country’s growth outlook f

or the rest of this year. However, this has not prevented several companies from pursuing their growth development plans. Chinalco Luoyang Copper, for example, will double its plate, sheet and strip capacity to 200kt/a by completing construction of its second plant by the end of this year. Zhejiang Hailiang Stock Co should become the world’s largest supplier of copper heat exchange tubing by the end of this year by expanding its capacity from 60kt/a to 90kt/a. Other product ranges already mean that the company’s copper and copper alloy tube capacity stands at 260kt/a+. Also, Fujian Nanping Sun Cable is pressing ahead with plans to build a 100kt/a copper rod facility in Shangang County. In a two-stage strategy, Fujian intends to build a 30kt/a rod line producing 8mm-dia product, among others, which should start up in September; a second line will add a further 70kt/a, with the total investment coming to 180M yuan. For this year we anticipate that China’s refined copper consumption will increase by a more moderate 5% to just under 5.27Mt. Demand for copper wire rod will continue to be supported by ongoing investment within the power sector while on the copper products side demand will continue to be boosted by the steady stream of new semis capacity due to come on line. However, given the poor global demand growth prospects, we anticipate Chinese growth of a further 5% only in 2010. While we talk about the economic crisis of 2008, we can in fact trace the start of the downturn in US copper consumption all the way back to Q2 2006, when housing starts began their decline. In 2007 US refined copper consumption continued to be hampered by the downturn in residential construction activity which was more prolonged and much sharper than many had anticipated, especially following the eruption of the sub-prime credit crisis in that August. Even so, the ongoing strength in the automotive sector still allowed national copper demand to increase that year by almost 2.8% on 2006, to 2.19Mt. Indeed, it was not until late-Q1 2008 that the real spectre of a sustained decline in copper data became evident, as virtually all copper-consuming sectors could not withstand any longer the underlining messag

e written by macro-economic collapse. As an example, from their peak of 128kt (metric - copper content) in March 2007, US brass mill shipments gradually tailed off over the course of the rest of that year, but still managed a reasonable 115kt in March 2008, according to data from the American Bureau of Statistics (ABMS). A typically strong September (100kt) seemed to defy the odds for another month, but the typically low December tally of just 59kt adequately summarised the degree of exhaustion in the sector, and compared poorly with the previous year’s end performance of 86kt. Equally, we saw a parallel performance from the copper wire rod sector, where production plunged to 79kt (metric) in December 2008 vs. 99kt a year prior, according to the ABMS. This brought the year on year decline to 8.4%, or 1.482Mt. Meanwhile, shipments of copper rod by US mills to domestic customers fell by 9% year on year to 1.46Mt (metric), fully one third lower than at the start of this decade. The poor market conditions brought even further contraction and rationalisation to the industry, following similar efforts in 2007. Following on from the Q4 closure of FMI/PD’s 120kt Hawthorne rod mill near Chicago and three other companies either close or embark on restructuring efforts at downstream facilities (such as winding/magnet wire), we expect that there will be some downtime, potentially further restructuring, ahead. During the forecast period (2009-2020) we forecast an overall decline in refined copper consumption in Europe from 2008’s 3.43Mt to 3.1Mt, an annual loss rate of 0.9%. This will reflect the loss of market share (for both copper wire rod and copper semi products) to the fast developing eastern European economies, the displacement of home grown copper-intensive white goods, as cheaper Chinese imports continue to flood the market, and the ongoing substitution of copper in some markets, particularly in plumbing tube applications, while copper prices remain high relative to competitors. _We forecast an overall decline in European demand during the forecast period_ ###### Japan By the end of 2008, it became clear that Japan had joined the ranks of economies in recession with confirmation that GDP contracted in the second and third quarters. The contraction was particularly acute in the third quarter and was a reflection of the country’s export-led businesses cutting production and investment in new capacity. Worryingly, another reason for the contraction was a sharp fall in government consumption. Consequently, Japanese demand for copper fell away by a further 5.4% last year, following the 3% year-on-year decline in 2007. At 1.2Mt for 2008, this leaves the sector virtually at 2003 levels, and our own prognosis anticipates no recovery until 2011. At the heart of the problem during 2008 was the widespread economic downturn that prompted several industrial indices and production performances to test Q4 lows last seen during the 1970s and even all the way back to when data recording began in the 1950s. The two principal semis production sectors that we follow - copper and brass alloy products, and wire and cable – continued to decline under the collapse of the m

_Troubled start to the year is setting the tone for most of 2009_ _Japanese demand for copper is expected to decline during the forecast period_ There seems to be little hope that the Japanese economy will improve dramatically this year, and so as recently as January we deemed it necessary to reduce our copper demand forecasts for the country to c.1Mt, which would represent a drop of almost 17% on 2008’s 1.2Mt. We learned that orders began the year down 50% on business levels of 12 months prior, with many brass mills operating at only 10% of capacity and wire rod producers operating at between 50-60% of capacity. As a consequence domestic cathode producers were delivering their unwanted material into LME warehouses for the first time ever. Essentially Japan’s export market has been devastated by the appreciation of the yen while domestic demand has been destroyed by the marked slowdown in the auto, housing and electrical and electronic sectors from October last year. Actual automotive _production_ levels continued reasonably strongly through to Q3, but outstripped _sales_ , thereby leaving a backlog that will need to be drawn down before new manufacturing can begin. The Japan Automobile Manufacturers’ projection that car sales will fall by 4.5% in 2009 is compounded by its forecast that domestic new car sales will fall by 4.9%, dropping below 5M units for the first time in 30 years. _Page 10_ _March 2009_ _Copper Executive Report_ _Brook Hunt_ ##### SECTION 4: GLOBAL PRODUCTION ###### Mine production Forecast mine by mine production levels are based on production capability. This is defined as the level of production that could reasonably be anticipated after allowing for normal disruptions. Extraordinary factors such as labour strikes, major plant failure and other unpredictable events are taken into account as a generic reduction in output until they can be allocated specifically against an individual operation. Production capability forecasts are based on mine plans where available but otherwise take into account known or anticipated technical developments relating to grade trends, stripping ratios, mining configuration and metallurgical performance. Projects that are almost certain to proceed to production but where the timing is still not confirmed are included as a separate project category in the production forecast. This is defined as the level of production that could reasonably be anticipated after allowing for normal disruptions. Extraordinary factors such as labour strikes, major plant failure and other unpredictable events are not taken into account on a plant-specific basis until actually realised. Individual production capability forecasts are based on planned output or set at a level that the smelter has demonstrably sustained. This may be less than the official capacity of the plant. Unlike cathodes, there is no terminal market (e.g. the LME) for copper concentrates and pricing is thus established through a process of negotiation between buyer and seller.  A copper concentrate smelting contract is drawn up between the buyer and seller to provide a framework covering a whole range of terms and conditions.  These include a treatment and refining charge, price participation (pp) – if any, payables for copper, silver and gold, penalties for impurities (e.g. arsenic, bismuth, fluorine, etc), quotational periods for payable metals and payment terms that the miner (or trader) will pay to the smelter (or trader) for smelting and refining services.  The main aspects of the contract that are subject to negotiation are the treatment and refining charges (TC/RCs) that are expressed in US dollars per dry met

ric tonne of concentrate (the TC) and in cents per pound of payable copper (the RC) and (under long-term contracts) pp. PP is a means whereby the buyer can participate in movements in the copper price above and often below agreed trigger prices.  PP is usually expressed as a percentage (typically 10%) participation while there may only be one trigger price (e.g. 90c/lb) or two prices (e.g. above $1/lb and below 80c/lb). 

Long-term contracts can cover one year, or many years (typically up to thirteen) and may be evergreen in nature (i.e. they continue to operate indefinitely after the initial term has been concluded).  Most long-term contracts are renegotiated annually during the so-called Mating Season looking at a supply/demand balance of twelve months forward.  This typically commences in September, and can continue through to April (or even later) the following year.  “Block” style contracts relate to 100% of the tonnage delivered during a calendar year while terms agreed under the more common “brick” pattern contracts apply to 50% of the following year and 50% to the year after and in this manner terms are established for 100% of the following year and 50% for the year after.  The concept of the brick contract is partly to attenuate the volatility of the market and partly to secure terms two years forward thereby reducing the risk of failing to reach agreement in non-holiday contracts. 

The custom concentrate market has been growing at an average rate of 4.9% p.a. since the mid-1990s while there has been virtually no net growth in the integrated sector.  During 2003 the size of the custom market exceeded that of the integrated sector for the first time.  In 2008 it is estimated that 54% was sold to third parties, compared with 46% consumed in integrated facilities (i.e. almost the same as in 2007). 

Approximately 74% (75% in 2007) of custom concentrates were traded internationally in 2008 with the remainder sold to smelters within the same country.  Merchants captured 30% (29%) of the custom market and 16% (16%) of the overall market in 2008. 

Six countries comprise almost 80% of the internationally traded custom concentrate market.  While Japan’s was the major consumer of custom concentrates its dominance has been eroded, from almost 40% of internationally traded material in 1996, to 29% in 2003, and 25% during 2006 and 2007 and to 24% in 2008.  China’s significance in this market has risen steadily and is now larger than Japan, having more than trebled from just 8% in 1996, to 25% presently.  India barely featured as a custom buyer in 1995, but rising domestic metal demand encouraged the construction of two large copper smelters that currently account for 11% of the international custom market. South Korea’s share has been fairly stable at 8-10% post 1998 following a major smelter expansion.  Other participants, in descending order of significance, are Germany, Spain, Philippines and Bulgaria.

##### SECTION 6:  TRENDS IN CONSUMPTION OF SECONDARY COPPER 

###### Scrap Definition 

_Copper scrap is classified into two categories_ 

Copper scrap is classified into two general categories called old and new scrap. New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply.  A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles.  New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. 

###### Scrapping Rates 

_Old scrap availability is linked to the volume of copper containing products_ 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in nonelectrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copp

er because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

###### Scrap Usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

_Some products can contain higher amounts of scrap than others_ 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases.

Copper prices were severely depressed for much of the period 1997-2003, with average 2002 quotes at their lowest level, measured in real terms, for over a century.  The initial catalyst for the downturn in prices was the Asian crisis that came about during 1997.  Subsequently the market had to contend with a severe US economic slowdown towards the end of 2000 that brought an end to one of the longest periods of US economic growth on record.  The impact of the US slowdown was accompanied by the implosion of the “I.T.” bubble in that country and elsewhere, leading to a particularly severe downturn in copper demand.  The US slowdown was felt across the globe with only one country, China, seemingly insulated from its effects.  The contraction in global copper demand, most notably in 2001 and 2002 and insufficient producer discipline in terms of reducing copper supplies prior to 2002, led to the accumulation of excessive metal inventories in exchange warehouses.  This situation was exacerbated by the relative strength of the US dollar against many other currencies, including those in a number of the major copper producing countries, such as Chile, Australia and Europe.  For mines in these regions low dollar copper prices actually translated into reasonable revenues when converted into depreciated local currencies. 

Additional supply was brought into production at a faster rate than was required by end users and so metal stocks in exchange warehouses continued to build, reaching record levels.  At the end of 1997 inventories on the LME, Comex and Shanghai exchanges amounted to 458kt.  By April 2002 these had ballooned to an all time high of 1.5Mt before declining to 1.3Mt by year-end.  Over that period more than 3Mt/a of copper mine capacity had been either closed or curtailed. At the same time, around 2.2Mt/a of greenfield and 2.4Mt/a of brownfield mine capacity was brought on stream, along with some of the curtailed mine capacity that was reactivated in response to weakening currencies against the US dollar.

A VAT rebate scheme on Chinese copper concentrate imports plus a 2% tariff on domestic Chinese copper metal sales also provided smelters in that country with substantial additional income that was not available to custom smelters elsewhere in the world.  As a consequence, custom concentrate sellers enjoyed some of the lowest treatment and refining charges on record over this period.

During 2004 global refined copper production increased by 4.3%, year on year, to just under 16Mt.  At the same time, refined copper consumption significantly outperformed the rise in supply with year-on-year growth of 9.4 % to ~17Mt, resulting in a global market deficit of around 1.1Mt Cu.  This abnormally high rate of consumption growth was in part due to robust economic growth and also due to a substantial consumer inventory correction (re-stocking). ##### SECTORAL ANALYSIS 

###### Automotive 

_Output to fall by at least 20%_ 

Car and commercial vehicle manufacturers are in the vanguard of the recession, with many – if not all – struggling for survival in the face of an unprecedented decline in sales.  The downturn has been remarkably sharp, synchronised and deep.  Even the most efficient manufacturers are laying off workers and increasing short-time working, postponing investment plans and curtailing marketing budgets. 

In such circumstances, quantifying the extent of the likely decline is extremely difficult.  Such was the extent of the decline in production through to year-end, global motor vehicle value added contracted by 4.6% in 2008 rather than the 0.5% fall envisaged in November (based on data through to September).  For 2009, a contraction of the order of 20% is now forecast, ahead of a rebound of around 8% in 2010. 

However, given the January indicators already starting to trickle through and the daily drip of dire corporate announcements, the risk remains that the contraction forecast for the first half of this year is still being underestimated. But the counterpart of this risk is that the rebound could be even larger than presently forecast…when it comes! At the moment, global production is predicted to take almost five years to return to recent peak levels, inevitably implying further manufacturer consolidation.  However, general fiscal and monetary policy stimuli plus specific measures to support the car sector could well spur a swifter rebound. 

In the context of such dramatic changes in global demand conditions, countryspecific events tend to be swamped.  In the US, GM and Chrysler have requested even more federal aid in recent days and the end-of-March deadline for a final decision on their restructuring plans – or resort to Chapter 11 – is looming.  Production in January slumped to 43.7% below its year-ago level as sales fell 39.7%.  In Japan, December production was down 34.5% year-on-year and similarly large declines were posted across Western Europe.

###### Electrical, electronics and computers Global economic weakness has clearly spread to the electronics and computers sector in recent months with contractionary forces particularly strong in the US and Asia. Final data indicate that last year’s expansion was a disappointingly weak 4.9% as significant downward momentum built up in the final months of the year. In 2009, output is expected to decline by 17% and, even in 2010, the rebound is a modest one to growth of 3.75%. _Recessionary pressures intensify_ The turnaround in the US has been swift, with output falling by 5.4% in the final quarter of 2008 alone – the first quarterly decline since Q1 2002. Computer production was already falling from mid-year but electronic components and consumer electronics went sharply into reverse in the final months of the year, while precision instruments and telecommunication equipment posted much more modest declines. The relative outperformance of the latter two sectors continued in January, when both saw production bounce back. However, the overall trend is clearly a contractionary one with order books generally dire. US output this year is seen falling 15%, in stark contrast to 2008’s 9.5% expansion. Across Asia, the speed of the deterioration has been even more dramatic. In Japan, production of electronics and computers fell for the fourth successive quarter and by a massive 16.3% in Q4 2008 alone, to stand 22.4% below its year-ago level. Here the declines have been more universal than in the US and, as a result, production is forecast to tumble by over 30% this year. Even in 2010, only a flat performance is envisaged as the yen’s strength exacerbates the shift to

production locations outside of Japan. For China, computer production for example fell sharply in the fourth quarter and Asian country trade data paint a clear picture of demand collapsing. In Europe, the speed and extent of the decline has been less marked, so far at least. Foreign orders have been hit hard but, for some countries and sectors, _March 2009_ _Page 55_ _Copper Executive Report_ _Brook Hunt_ domestic orders have only very recently started to move lower. Moreover, just as growth rates had been less dynamic, so the declines should not be as large as those in the US and Asia. For example, fourth-quarter data for the West only reduced full-year growth for 2008 to 3.1% from the forecast 3.5% rate. For this year, a 7% decline is forecast for both Western and Eastern Europe.
